guideTitle: Best Solar Generators for a 50 Amp RV Outlet (2026)
metaTitle: Solar Generators for a 50 Amp RV Outlet
metaDescription: Six solar generators for 50 amp motorhomes and fifth wheels, built around a load-shedding plan for which circuits to keep alive on 120V and 240V.
expertTake: The EcoVolt P5000 Plus is the best pick for a 50 amp coach that wants a big tank, since its 5,120Wh and 120/240V output cover both legs at a moderate cost. The Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is the safer long-term buy if you value support and expansion. Skip any single 3,600W unit if your plan includes both rooftop air conditioners, because the load math does not close.
introParagraphs: A fifty amp motorhome or fifth wheel is wired as two halves, and the useful way to think about a battery is to decide which half of the coach you want alive and for how long. The outlet is where the batteries meet that plan, and the plan matters more than the connector.

This guide starts with load-shedding: which circuits are worth keeping, which should be left dark and what that implies for a battery's voltage, output and tank. The six machines below are ordered by how well they serve that plan in a coach with the usual roof air conditioners.

products.name: EcoVolt P5000 Plus 5,120Wh 120/240V Power Station
products.description:
The P5000 Plus makes the case for energy over power. Its inverter is rated 3,600W with a 5,000W surge, which is enough for one rooftop air conditioner, the refrigerator and the kitchen, and its dual-voltage output means a coach panel sees both legs. The real asset is the 5,120Wh tank, the biggest single-unit tank in the group.

In a motorhome that translates to a real afternoon of cooling plus an evening of cooking, two things smaller batteries struggle to combine. The listing quotes 1,800W of AC input and 1,000W of solar input, so a hookup lunch or a good sun day recovers a lot of charge.

The cost of the value is brand history, so test the unit with real loads when it arrives and keep the receipt. Against the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus it holds 1,536Wh more energy but lacks the established support network. Keep it dry and ventilated, and store it half charged. Because it has five AC outlets, you can run short heavy-gauge leads to each circuit group instead of daisy-chaining power strips, which keeps voltage drop low. In practice the 3,600W ceiling means you stagger the microwave and the air conditioner instead of running them together, and the large tank forgives that discipline. Several owners pair it with a small second battery for electronics so the big inverter can stay idle overnight and save its idle draw.
products.bestFor: Motorhome owners who want the biggest tank and both legs live at a moderate cost.
pros: 5,120Wh is the largest single-unit tank here
cons: Brand has a short track record

products.name: BLUETTI Apex 300 with B300K Battery and Hub D1
products.description:
Where the P5000 Plus is one big box, the Apex 300 is a system you assemble. A single unit provides 3,840W and gives 120V and 240V at the same time, and the listing says two or three can be paralleled for 5.5 to 8.3kWh. For a coach that grows with its owner, that is attractive: start with one air conditioner's worth of power and add batteries as you learn.

The bundle includes a DC hub with a 50A Anderson port, two cigarette lighter ports and USB-C ports, which suits the 12V side of a motorhome and makes it more than an AC box. The 2,764.8Wh capacity is modest on its own, so expect to buy the second module quickly.

Set up the stack on a firm shelf, label every cable and follow the maker's parallel instructions exactly. Check connectors for tightness each season and keep the units dry. Because each module is a separate heavy box, plan the stack height and make sure the lowest shelf can carry the full weight. Compared with a single-box rival, the main upside is redundancy: if one module needs service, the others keep the coach partially powered. The main downside is that each extra module weighs about as much as a small suitcase of bricks, so lifting gear is part of the plan.
products.bestFor: Owners who prefer to scale a system module by module.
pros: DC hub with a 50A Anderson port

products.name: Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus with 2x200W Panels
products.description:
For a coach owner who cares about warranty and long-term parts, the HomePower 3600 Plus is the conservative pick. One unit supplies 3,600W on a single leg, two in parallel reach 7,200W and expansion goes to 21kWh. The heat-resistant ceramic membrane cells matter in a motorhome bay that sees summer sun.

In load-shedding terms, one unit feeds one half of the coach: the refrigerator, converter, outlets and one air conditioner on that leg. The listing describes a plug-and-play house connection through a manual transfer switch, so the same battery can serve the home in an outage.

Two 200W panels are included, which is modest for a 3,584Wh tank. Keep the vents clear, store it half charged and test the paired setup under load before a long trip. Ask your installer whether the coach's transfer switch can be reconfigured to accept a battery input, since many motorhomes use an automatic one built for a generator. Of the group it is the one most likely to still be supported and serviceable after a decade of ownership, which is worth a premium if you plan to keep the coach for years.
products.bestFor: Owners who want an established brand and a path to a paired system.
cons: Single unit covers one leg only
Higher cost than the P5000 Plus

products.name: ABOK Ark3600 with 3x200W Solar Panels and TT-30 Port
products.description:
If the question is which battery brings its own panels, the answer is this kit. Three 200W panels give about 1,900Wh on a good day, which keeps a coach's refrigerator, lights and electronics running indefinitely, and the TT-30 port gives a native 30 amp connection for the common adapter route to a 50 amp inlet. The unit also lists 15 output ports and a 7,200W peak, so a coach with many small circuits finds a socket for everything.

In a 50 amp coach it is a single-leg 120V machine at 3,600W, so it carries one half of the loads. A common arrangement is the refrigerator, the microwave, the converter and the front air conditioner on that leg, with the rear air conditioner and the electric water heater left off. The 3,840Wh tank is 1,280Wh smaller than the P5000 Plus's but arrives with the solar side solved, and expansion to 11,520Wh gives a growth path.

The panels are rigid and bulky, so plan a ground mount, a roof rack or a stow location for them. The 3,600W rating is the circuit's peak, so plan around 2,880W continuous, strap the unit down and check the cord for heat after the first long run. Check panel cables after each trip, keep connectors clean and store the battery at half charge. One practical tip is to carry the panels in a cargo bay sleeve so the glass survives travel, since replacement panels in this class are not cheap.
products.bestFor: Boondockers who want panels and a TT-30 port in one purchase.
pros: TT-30 port for the adapter route
Fast combined AC and solar input
cons: Rigid panels are awkward to store

products.name: Jackery Solar Generator 300 with 40W Solar Panel
products.description:
A small battery earns a spot in a big coach when it takes the little jobs off the big battery. Phones, laptops, a router and a fan can run from this 7.5 pound unit, so the 3,600W machine is free to handle air conditioning and cooking.

It is not a coach battery in its own right, since 292Wh and 300W cannot run a refrigerator overnight or any appliance with a heating element. Think of it as the overnight desk and bedside battery for the people in the rig.

Its 100W USB-C PD port charges a laptop efficiently, and the LiFePO4 pack is rated over 4,000 cycles. Leave it near half charge and out of hot compartments. One neat use is a dedicated overnight charger for a CPAP without a heated humidifier, which draws only 30 to 50Wh a night. Because it is so light, it also serves as an emergency battery in the tow vehicle for jump-starting phones and tablets on a long drive.
products.bestFor: Coach owners who want a portable second battery for electronics.
pros: Takes small loads off the main battery
cons: Not a substitute for the main battery

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 50 amp coach has two legs. Put the refrigerator, converter and one air conditioner on one leg and treat the second air conditioner and the electric water heater as optional. A 3,600W single-leg unit like the HomePower 3600 Plus or ABOK Ark3600 covers one leg, the P5000 Plus's dual voltage covers both.

A 15,000 BTU roof unit draws about 1,500W running and 3,000W at start. Two of them pull about 3,000W running, which already hits the 2,880W continuous guideline on a 3,600W inverter. The P5000 Plus's 5,000W surge helps, but only one runs comfortably. Soft-start kits on the roof units cut the starting spike by about half and are the cheapest upgrade in this whole plan.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Tank size for a full afternoon
buyingCriteria.explanation: One air conditioner at 1,500W plus 300W for the refrigerator and lights drains 3,840Wh in about two hours. The P5000 Plus's 5,120Wh gives nearly three, and a stacked Apex 300 at 8.3kWh gives about four and a half. Remember that cooling load climbs with outside temperature, so a mild morning's runtime will not hold at three in the afternoon.
Coaches run lights, water pumps and slide motors on 12V. The Apex 300's DC hub with a 50A Anderson port feeds it directly, saving inverter and converter losses of about 10 to 15 percent.

The ABOK kit's 600W of panels refills about 1,900Wh a day and the P5000 Plus accepts 1,000W. A motorhome can also recharge from its engine alternator through a DC-to-DC charger, which beats panels on travel days. A DC-to-DC alternator charger rated around 500W adds roughly 1,500Wh over a three-hour drive.

A 5,000Wh battery weighs over 100 pounds. In a coach, mount it low, near the axle and strapped to a structural member. Check the cargo bay's weight rating before you buy. Heavy batteries behind the rear axle also change handling, so keep them forward of it where you can.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to a load-shedding plan
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged each unit against a plan of one air conditioner, refrigerator and kitchen. Dual-voltage units scored highest, with single-leg units credited for half the coach.

howWeEvaluated.title: Afternoon runtime
howWeEvaluated.description: We estimated hours at 1,800W with a 0.85 factor. The P5000 Plus gives about 2.4 hours, the ABOK 1.8 and the Apex 300 about 1.3 per unit. We used the same two-hour benchmark for every unit so the comparison is fair.

howWeEvaluated.title: 12V integration
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for DC hubs and RV ports. The Apex 300 and the ABOK TT-30 kit stood out.

howWeEvaluated.title: Refill options
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared included panels and input limits. The ABOK kit's 600W and the P5000 Plus's 1,000W input led.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We drew on the listings and owner feedback patterns for weight and support, not our own use. We also weighed how easy it is to move a unit for service.

howToChoose.subheading: Big Single Tank vs Stackable Modules

cards.label: Big single tank
cards.text: The P5000 Plus gives 5,120Wh in one box. It is simple, cheaper per watt-hour and has no cabling to manage.

cards.label: Stackable modules
cards.text: The Apex 300 and HomePower 3600 Plus grow in steps. You can start smaller and spread cost, but each module adds weight and cabling.

howToChoose.note: Choose a single tank for simplicity and modules if your needs will change.

howToChoose.subheading: For Fifth Wheels and Motorhomes Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a battery whose weight you can place low in a cargo bay, plus the ability to feed the coach panel without cord gymnastics. Check the bay's weight rating.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The P5000 Plus and Apex 300 both suit a bay, and the HomePower 3600 Plus's brand support is useful on the road.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You boondock for days in hot weather. The Apex 300 stack or the P5000 Plus pays off.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You camp at powered sites. A single ABOK Ark3600 covers outages.

maintenance.why: A labelled map of which circuits sit on each leg saves guesswork when you shed loads. Keep a copy of the labels in the coach's manual folder so anyone driving can find them.
A heavy battery shifting in a moving coach is a safety hazard and damages the case.
LiFePO4 cells age slowest at moderate charge. Top it up every two to three months so the battery management system keeps its reading accurate.
Dust limits full-load runtime in a warm bay.
Anderson and DC5521 connectors loosen with vibration. A dab of dielectric grease keeps corrosion off the terminals in humid climates.

faq.q: Can I run both roof air conditioners?
faq.a: Only briefly. Two units pull about 3,000W running and more at start, which uses most of a 3,600W inverter. A 5,120Wh tank lasts under two hours that way. Staggering the two starts by a few minutes avoids the combined surge.

faq.q: Do I need 240V for a 50 amp coach?
faq.a: Not for everything. A 120V unit can feed one leg. For both legs, choose the P5000 Plus or Apex 300. Read your coach's panel schedule to see which loads sit on which leg before you decide.

The EcoVolt P5000 Plus gives the largest tank and dual voltage for the least outlay. Treat the brand as a risk and keep the receipt. The Apex 300 costs more but scales, which can make it the cheaper path if your needs grow.

faq.q: Can I charge from the engine alternator?
faq.a: Yes with a DC-to-DC charger sized for the battery. The ABOK bundle in this group includes a 500W version in a related listing. Wiring needs a fuse and proper gauge. Ask a qualified installer to check wire gauge and fusing before you connect.

faq.q: How do I keep the battery from overheating in the bay?
faq.a: Leave an air gap, avoid sealed cupboards and keep the vents clear. Heat shortens battery life and limits full-load runtime. A small 12V fan in the bay can add useful airflow for very little power.

faq.q: Do panels need to be on the roof?
faq.a: No. Ground-mounted panels can be tilted and shifted with the sun, and they leave the roof free. A longer cable run costs a few percent.
